topic.title: Learning with Unlabeled Data and Unreliable Supervision
topic.overview: Labels may be scarce, noisy, partial, or supplied by a weaker model. This topic studies how unlabeled structure, consistency, generative label models, and selective trust can compensate for those imperfections. A central problem is distinguishing genuinely informative agreement from mutually reinforcing errors.
topic.whyItMatters: Additional unlabeled data help only when the assumptions connecting them to the target labels are useful. Noisy supervision can be memorized, and distribution differences can make consistency harmful. Methods therefore need to account for how labels were sampled, which examples are difficult, and when a teacher should be trusted.
topic.evolution: A 1993 method uses agreement across sensory modalities as a substitute for some supervision. Later work develops local-global consistency and perturbation-based semi-supervision. Early-learning regularization in 2020 addresses noisy-label memorization; a 2026 label-diffusion approach predicts labels directly and uses historical inconsistency to adapt treatment of clean, noisy, and hard examples.
openQuestions: How can consistency methods detect shared mistakes across models or modalities?
What evidence supports trusting weak labels on examples unlike the labeled training set?
